title: B1 Writing Quiz 2 — Media, Opinions & Social Life

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: If I were famous, I wouldn't post everything online.
If I am famous, I wouldn't post everything online.
If I were famous, I won't post everything online.
If I would be famous, I wouldn't post everything online.
questions.explanation: Second conditional: If + past simple, would + base verb: 'If I were famous, I wouldn't post everything online.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: If she had read the reviews, she wouldn't watch that film.
If she had read the reviews, she wouldn't have watched that film.
If she read the reviews, she wouldn't have watched that film.
If she would have read the reviews, she wouldn't have watched that film.
questions.explanation: Third conditional: If + past perfect, would have + past participle: 'If she had read..., she wouldn't have watched...'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: This magazine is read by millions of people.
This magazine reads by millions of people.
This magazine is reading by millions of people.
This magazine read by millions of people.
questions.explanation: Present simple passive: is/are + past participle: 'is read by millions of people.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The article was published last Friday.
The article published last Friday.
The article was publish last Friday.
The article is published last Friday.
questions.explanation: Past simple passive: was/were + past participle: 'was published last Friday.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The influencer who started the trend has millions of followers.
The influencer which started the trend has millions of followers.
The influencer whom started the trend has millions of followers.
The influencer, who started the trend, has millions of followers but.
questions.explanation: 'Who' introduces a defining relative clause about a person: 'The influencer who started the trend...'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: My favorite podcast, which airs weekly, just hit one million listeners.
My favorite podcast which airs weekly just hit one million listeners but.
My favorite podcast, that airs weekly, just hit one million listeners.
My favorite podcast which airs weekly, just hit one million listeners.
questions.explanation: Non-defining relative clauses use commas and 'which' for things: 'My favorite podcast, which airs weekly, just hit one million listeners.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: That story can't be true, it sounds too strange.
That story can't to be true, it sounds too strange.
That story can't being true, it sounds too strange.
That story cann't be true, it sounds too strange.
questions.explanation: 'Can't' + base verb expresses a confident negative deduction: 'that story can't be true.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The article could be exaggerating the facts.
The article could being exaggerating the facts.
The article could to be exaggerating the facts.
The article coulds be exaggerating the facts.
questions.explanation: 'Could' + base verb expresses a possible deduction: 'the article could be exaggerating.'

questions.topic: Present perfect vs present perfect continuous
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I've watched five episodes today.
I've been watching five episodes today.
I've watch five episodes today.
I'm watching five episodes today already.
questions.explanation: Present perfect simple is used for a completed number of results: 'I've watched five episodes.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I've been following that debate for months.
I've followed that debate since months.
I'm following that debate for months already.
I've been follow that debate for months.
questions.explanation: Present perfect continuous emphasizes duration of an unfinished action: 'I've been following... for months.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence. (Direct: "I have shared the article.")
options: She said that she has shared the article.
She said that she had shared the article.
She said that she shared the article already.
She said she have shared the article.
questions.explanation: In reported speech, present perfect shifts back to past perfect: 'she had shared the article.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence. (Direct: "What do you think of the news?")
options: He asked me what do I think of the news.
He asked me what I thought of the news.
He asked me what did I think of the news.
He asked me what I think of the news.
questions.explanation: Reported questions use normal word order (no auxiliary inversion) and shift the tense back: 'he asked me what I thought of the news.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I used to watch the news every evening before I got my phone.
I use to watch the news every evening before I got my phone.
I was used to watch the news every evening before I got my phone.
I used to watching the news every evening before I got my phone.
questions.explanation: 'Used to' + base verb describes a past habit that no longer happens: 'I used to watch the news every evening.'

questions.topic: Be used to / get used to
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I'm used to scrolling through the news every morning.
I'm used to scroll through the news every morning.
I use to scrolling through the news every morning.
I'm used scrolling to through the news every morning.
questions.explanation: 'Be used to' is followed by a gerund: 'I'm used to scrolling through the news.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: She always brings up controversial topics at dinner.
She always brings controversial topics up at dinner away.
She always brings up to controversial topics at dinner.
She always brings controversial topics at dinner up.
questions.explanation: 'Bring up' means 'mention or introduce a topic': 'brings up controversial topics.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The journalist decided to look into the rumors.
The journalist decided to look the rumors into.
The journalist decided to look into to the rumors.
The journalist decided to look rumors into the.
questions.explanation: 'Look into' means 'investigate': 'look into the rumors.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Despite the criticism, the show remained popular.
Despite of the criticism, the show remained popular.
Although the criticism, the show remained popular.
Despite the criticism was strong, the show remained popular.
questions.explanation: 'Despite' is followed by a noun phrase (no 'of'): 'Despite the criticism, the show remained popular.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The post went viral. As a result, thousands of people commented.
The post went viral, as a result thousands of people commented.
As a result the post went viral thousands of people commented.
The post went viral as a result, thousands of people commented.
questions.explanation: 'As a result' starts a new sentence and is followed by a comma: 'The post went viral. As a result, thousands of people commented.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The article doesn't give enough evidence for its claims.
The article doesn't give evidence enough for its claims.
The article doesn't give enough of evidence for its claims.
The article hasn't enough evidence for its claims.
questions.explanation: 'Enough' comes before the noun it modifies: 'enough evidence.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Most readers were in favour of the new policy.
Most readers were in favour for the new policy.
Most readers were favour of the new policy.
Most readers were on favour of the new policy.
questions.explanation: 'In favour of' + noun means 'supporting': 'in favour of the new policy.'

questions.question: Which is the correct way to start an email to a magazine editor you haven't met, proposing an article?
options: Hey there,
Dear Editor,
Yo,
Hiya,
questions.explanation: 'Dear Editor,' is a suitable formal opening when the recipient's exact name is unknown.

questions.question: Which is the correct way to end a formal email pitching an idea to a named contact?
options: Yours faithfully,
Kind regards,
Later,
Talk soon,
questions.explanation: 'Kind regards,' is a suitable semi-formal closing when writing to a named professional contact.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I was wondering if you could share your source for the article.
I was wondering if you could to share your source for the article.
I was wondering could you sharing your source for the article.
I wonder if you share could your source for the article.
questions.explanation: 'I was wondering if you could' + base verb is a polite way to make a request: 'if you could share your source.'

questions.question: Which sentence correctly combines 'This is the author.' and 'The author's book became a bestseller.'?
options: This is the author whose book became a bestseller.
This is the author who book became a bestseller.
This is the author which book became a bestseller.
This is the author's book who became a bestseller.
questions.explanation: 'Whose' shows possession in a relative clause: 'the author whose book became a bestseller.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I have never shared such a personal post before.
I have shared never such a personal post before.
Never I have shared such a personal post before.
I have shared such a personal post never before.
questions.explanation: 'Never' is placed between the auxiliary and the past participle: 'I have never shared such a post.'

questions.question: Which sentence has correct punctuation?
options: I'd like to know whether the interview has been published.
I'd like to know whether has the interview been published?
I'd like to know, whether the interview has been published.
I'd like to know whether the interview has been published?
questions.explanation: Reported/indirect statements use normal word order and end with a full stop, not a question mark.

questions.question: This time tomorrow, I ___ the live broadcast at the studio.
options: will watch
will be watching
am watching
watch
questions.explanation: Future continuous describes an action in progress at a specific future time: 'will be watching'.

questions.question: By the end of the year, this channel ___ over ten million subscribers.
options: will reach
will have reached
reaches
is reaching
questions.explanation: Future perfect describes an action completed before a future point: 'will have reached'.

questions.question: Choose the sentence that correctly uses discourse markers.
options: Firstly, check the source. Secondly, compare other reports. Finally, form your opinion.
Firstly we check source secondly compare finally opinion.
Finally check the source, firstly compare, secondly form opinion.
Secondly firstly check source, finally compare opinion.
questions.explanation: Discourse markers 'Firstly,', 'Secondly,' and 'Finally,' organize points clearly with commas.

questions.question: Choose the correct question tag.
options: You wouldn't share fake news, would you?
You wouldn't share fake news, do you?
You wouldn't share fake news, wouldn't you?
You wouldn't share fake news, will you?
questions.explanation: Negative statement with 'would' + positive tag: 'you wouldn't share..., would you?'
